name: Commercial broiler chicken raising on the Delmarva Peninsula
summary: From 1923 farmers on the Delmarva Peninsula began raising large flocks of young chickens purely for meat, an early start of the commercial broiler industry.
description: In 1923 Cecile Steele of Ocean View, Delaware, who kept hens for eggs, was sent 500 chicks instead of 50 and raised them for meat, selling 387 birds at 62 cents a pound. She ordered 1,000 chicks in 1924, had built a broiler house for 10,000 birds by 1926 and was selling 26,000 birds a year by 1928, and neighbouring farmers in Delaware and on the Eastern Shore followed. A university extension account says such specialised broiler operations were still too few in the 1920s and 1930s to change the supply of chicken meat.

impact.note: The sources show the practice spreading through Delmarva and the United States broiler trade, one society, and poultry keeping there was reorganised from eggs to meat; descent of the later integrated and worldwide industry from Delmarva in particular is not sourced, so reach and generativity take the lower score.

why: A hatchery sent ten times the chicks ordered and the surplus was raised for meat; neighbouring farmers hit by crop blights then copied the profitable result.

date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: In 1923 Mrs. Wilmer Steele (Cecile Steele) of Sussex County, Delaware, raised a flock of 500 chicks to be sold for meat; the Delaware source places her at Ocean View.

evidence.supports: Mrs. Wilmer Steele of Sussex County, Delaware, is often cited as the pioneer of the commercial broiler industry. In 1923, she raised a flock of 500 chicks intended to be sold for meat.

date.label: by 1926
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: By 1926 Steele had built a broiler house with room for 10,000 birds.

evidence.supports: Her little business was so profitable that, by 1926, Mrs. Steele was able to build a broiler house with a capacity of 10,000 birds.

date.label: by 1928
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Steele ordered 1,000 chicks in 1924 and by 1928 was selling 26,000 birds a year.

evidence.supports: The budding entrepreneur ordered 1,000 chicks in 1924. By 1928, she was selling 26,000 birds a year.

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Both sources for the Steele flock are promotional or trade-association pages; an archive, National Register or agricultural-history source for 1923 and for the 1926 broiler house would be stronger.
Whether specialised broiler flocks in Georgia, Arkansas or New England predate 1923 is unsettled.

The steps that made this intensive farming in the full sense of the concept (vitamin D and formulated feed, the Chicken of Tomorrow contests of 1946–1951, antibiotics, vertical integration by the 1960s) are not sourced here and need their own records.

research.note: The National Chicken Council says Steele 'is often cited as the pioneer of the commercial broiler industry' but also that broiler production began in Georgia, Arkansas and New England as well, and that a few farmers sold young meat chickens as a sideline around 1900, so priority is not shown.
